event.description: Frances Loeb Library Faculty Author Talk Please join us in the library for a conversation between Hannah Ahlblad and Jorge Otero-Pailos on Treaties on De-Fences. Treaties on De-Fences is an artist book of prints created by Jorge Otero-Pailos and made available to the public on the occasion of his 2024 Park Avenue sculptures exhibition Analogue Sites. Much like the exhibition, the artist’s book of prints aims to raise awareness and advocate for the preservation of modernist U.S. embassies. While the art installation uses large sculptures, as a method to make these embassies visible and tangible to the general public, the artist's book of prints further enacts and intertwines the energy of the sculptures and the diplomatic treaties from which the sculptures derive their names. This event is free and open to the public. Participants are invited to attend in person in the Loeb Library or join via livestream, here. This event will be recorded.
event.title: Treaties on De-Fences

event.description: FACULTY AUTHOR TALK "Expanding the Blueprint in a Man-Made World” Evolution, Longevity, and Leadership in Training and Practice Please join in the library for a conversation of MDE Design Lecturer Karen Korellis Reuther with Dean Sarah Whiting and Professor Belinda Tato on the recent publication, Man-Made: How We Designed a World That Leaves Women Out, and How We Can Make It Right with Harper Business. Drawing on more than four decades of experience as an industrial designer and leader at companies including Nike and Reebok, design critic in advanced studies at the Harvard Graduate School of Design (GSD), Karen Korellis Reuther examines how products, spaces, and systems have often been designed around male bodies and experiences, leaving women to navigate environments that can be uncomfortable, exclusionary, or unsafe. The book argues for a more expansive approach to design that treats inclusion not as an add-on, but as a fundamental responsibility of the design process. This event will be held in the Frances Loeb Library and will be streamed and recorded.
event.title: Expanding the Blueprint in a Man-Made World

event.description: Featuring Ana María León.Ana María León’s work traces how spatial practices and transnational networks of power and resistance shape the modernity and coloniality of the Americas. Her research and teaching foregrounds the agency of populations under struggle and the multiple forms of bias embedded in the built environment and its histories. León is invested in collaborative approaches to learning, teaching, and writing. Attention to multiple critical positions, particularly those of historically underrepresented groups, she argues, grounds our understanding of history in the politics of coliberation. About _positions Where do you stand in the field of architecture? “_positions” is a series of conversations convened by the Department of Architecture at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design aimed at revealing the positions – temporary, relational, and self-conscious – taken by players on the field of contemporary architecture. Participating GSD faculty and invited guests are drawn from all facets of the discipline – architects, designers, historians, scholars, theorists, technologists, and those in other allied fields. The notion of relationality supersedes any fixed number of speakers. All speakers are asked to discharge the same task: share three projects that correspond to the development of your position over time. Each speaker’s three projects are selected and regarded as answers to a series of guiding questions. First, what project by a mentor or teacher or school of thought informed the position you occupy today? (Where did your position come from and to whom or what do you owe your line of thinking?) Second, what project of your own was the first to indicate your position? (Where did your position begin and how did it define your stance in a particular spot?) event.description: In landscapes without land—interior gardens, green roofs, and constructed wetlands—ecological interactions unfold within anthropogenic strata of polymers, aggregates, concrete, and steel. These engineered environments can bring life to otherwise inert sites. Yet, they are places of vegetal deviation rather than conformity: plants are expected to exceed the conventional limits of their natural habits and appearances. The feedback loops between technology and life are tightly bound—and the evolution of a landscape can be misread as failure if it does not conform to a priori expectations. From gardens to infrastructural landscapes, practitioners design and maintain material systems to cultivate particular forms of biological variation—while foreclosing others. As both cautionary tales and design possibilities, projects that work “beyond” nature call for two forms of sustained attention. The first is to follow technologized forms of life through periods of unruliness, asking what these non-human entities and humans might accomplish together that neither could achieve alone. The second is to confront what accountability for such living systems could entail—and to recognize how attending to the full life cycle of a landscape can unsettle institutional conventions governing material systems, potentially bringing designers and the public closer to projects of regeneration rather than mere replacement. —Danielle Choi, Associate Professor of Landscape Architecture
event.title: Danielle Choi, "Design Beyond Nature"

event.description: Following the Kengo Kuma in Conversation _positions lecture with Grace La about Kuma's latest publication, KENGO KUMA: NEW WORKS, a book signing will take place afterward in the Frances Loeb Library. Books will be available for sale in the Druker Gallery before and after the lecture. More information about the event can be found on the GSD website. Kengo Kuma was born in 1954. He proposes architecture that opens up new relationships between nature, technology, and human beings, and established Kengo Kuma & Associates (KKAA) in 1990. The firm currently has projects underway in more than 50 countries. Kuma is a University Professor and Professor Emeritus at the University of Tokyo, after teaching at Keio University. His major publications include KENGO KUMA New Works, Kengo Kuma Onomatopoeia Architecture Grounding (X-Knowledge), Nihon no Kenchiku (Architecture of Japan, Iwanami Shoten), Zen Shigoto (Kengo Kuma,Complete Works, Daiwa Shobo), Ten Sen Men (Point Line Plane, Iwanami Shoten), Makeru Kenchiku (Architecture of Defeat, Iwanami Shoten), Shizen na Kenchiku (Natural Architecture, Iwanami Shinsho), Chii-sana Kenchiku (Small Architecture, Iwanami Shinsho), and many others. Grace La is Professor and Chair of the department of architecture at the Harvard University Graduate School of Design. She is cofounding principal of LA DALLMAN, a practice recognized for integrating architecture, engineering, and landscape. LA DALLMAN engages in catalytic projects of diverse scale–including civic spaces, bridges, houses, historic and mid-century modern buildings. The practice has received numerous professional honors and has presented at the National Building Museum, the New Museum, the Danish Architectural Museum, the Carnegie Museum of Art, the Houston MFA, the Chicago Architecture Biennial, and others. event.description: Hannah Greenwald Healy - Harvard University The rate of infectious disease outbreaks is increasing globally and in the U.S. due to factors like international travel, climate shifts, and declining vaccination rates. Environmental surveillance— the systematic testing of water or air for health-relevant markers— can complement clinical surveillance infrastructure, often providing early warning and more comprehensive data on infectious disease trends. In this talk, Dr. Healy will describe the resurgence in wastewater surveillance during the COVID-19 pandemic and her work since then to advance the technology and expand to new targets. Next, she will discuss how environmental monitoring and cleaning practices can reduce exposures to waterborne pathogens in healthcare environments. Finally, she will discuss her lab’s work on expanding the utility of wastewater surveillance to unsewered settings, including communities in the Peruvian Amazon. Together, these studies demonstrate how environmental surveillance can support infectious disease management through water system management, infection prevention, and public health response. Hannah Greenwald Healy has been an Assistant Professor of Environmental Health and Exposure Science at the Harvard T.H. Chan School of Public Health since January 2025, where she runs the Healy Health ‘Omics (H2O) Lab. She holds a secondary appointment in the Department of Environmental Science and Engineering and is Associate Faculty at the Broad Institute. Dr. Healy is trained as an Environmental Engineer, receiving her B.S. from Georgia Tech and M.S. and Ph.D. from the University of California, Berkeley. Prior to her faculty appointment, she completed a Gaylord Donnelley Postdoctoral Fellowship at Yale University in the Department of Chemical and Environmental Engineering. event.description: Rajan Chakrabarty - Washington University Light-absorbing carbonaceous aerosols (LACs)—encompassing both black and brown carbon—significantly influence atmospheric thermodynamics, surface temperatures, and cloud microphysics. The absence of consensus on the properties of LACs across their lifecycle, from emission to atmospheric processing to deposition, is one of the grand challenges in atmospheric aerosol science. Large discrepancies exist between directly measured LAC properties and their parameterizations in current models. To classify the complex optical properties of LACs, researchers increasingly rely on a brown-black continuum model. Along this spectrum, the imaginary part of the refractive index (k), which dictates light absorption, varies by orders of magnitude. At one extreme lies water-soluble brown carbon (BrC), which is weakly absorbing and highly susceptible to photobleaching. At the opposite end is black carbon (BC), defined by strong, wavelength-independent absorption across the visible and infrared spectra. Bridging this gap is dark BrC—highly refractory, water-insoluble particles with shortwave absorption efficiencies rivaling BC. In this seminar, I will explore the physicochemical dynamics of the LAC brown-black continuum, beginning with combustion-driven formation and the resulting particle characteristics. I will then pivot to contemporary measurement techniques for aerosol microphysics, highlighting advanced instrumental and computational methods for quantifying wavelength-dependent refractive indices and optical cross-sections. Finally, I will discuss recent advancements in applying these foundational insights to stratospheric solar radiation management. Dr. Rajan K. Chakrabarty is the Harold D. Jolley Professor of Engineering at Washington University in St. Louis, where he directs the Aerosol Interdisciplinary Research (AIR) Laboratory. Something similar is true with generative AI and large language models (LLMs): their successes involve both powerful observable behavior as well as deep internal representations of the world that they construct for their own uses. How do these internal representations work, and how similar or different are they compared to the representations of the world that we build as humans? This distinction is becoming crucial as people interact with powerful AI systems, where a mismatch between the system's model of the world and our human models of the world can lead to situations in which the system inadvertently `sets us up to fail' through our interactions with it. We explore these questions through the lens of generative AI, drawing on examples from game-playing, geographic navigation, and other complex tasks: When we train a model to win chess games, what happens when we pair it with a weaker partner who makes some of the moves? When we train a model to find shortest driving routes, what happens when it has to deal with unexpected detours? The picture we construct is further complicated by theoretical results indicating that successful generation can be achieved even by agents that are provably incapable of identifying the model they're generating from. event.description: Title: A vision for AI that makes us stronger Abstract: AI is often framed as a race for speed: replace human labor with computation, produce more, finish faster. event.description: Title: What Does Safety Mean for Generalist Robots? Speaker: Andrea Bajcsy, Assistant Professor in the Robotics Institute at Carnegie Mellon University Abstract: Robot safety is a nuanced concept. We commonly equate safety with collision-avoidance. However, when considering the possibility of generalist robots -- one robot that can do "anything" -- we need to expand our notion of safety. For example, a manipulator should understand when it is not confident about a requested task, that objects should be gently manipulated to prevent breaking or spilling, and that overheating items can cause burning or melting. However, designing robots that have such a nuanced safety understanding (and that can reliably generate appropriate actions) is an outstanding challenge. In this talk, I will describe my group's work on systematically uniting modern machine learning models (such as large vision-language models and latent world models) with classical formulations of safety in the control literature to generalize safe robot decision-making to increasingly open world interactions. Throughout the talk, I will present experimental instantiations of these ideas in domains like vision-based robotic manipulation. event.description: Engineering materials are selected for fixed properties and then protected with safety factors, because repeated loading degrades them. Living structural materials do the opposite: bone senses mechanical loading and converts it into mineral deposition where stiffness is needed, while coral self-stiffens as waves cement its skeleton. This talk asks whether synthetic materials can likewise use mechanical loading itself as the signal that improves them and presents two complementary routes toward that goal. The first route grows material in response to load. Cyclic loading of piezoelectric scaffolds in an electrolyte generates surface charges that drive mineralization in proportion to stress. The resulting composites gain both stiffness and energy-dissipation capacity under the very cyclic loading that would normally fatigue them, and the growth is self-limiting, with a saturation thickness set by the applied force. Recent results show that force also controls the nucleation density, crystallization kinetics, and hardness of the mineral, pointing to mechanical energy as a general lever for directing crystallization. The second route architects the response to load. Lattices built from liquid crystal elastomers couple snap-through buckling of tilted beams with the rate-dependent soft elasticity of mesogen rotation. The result is a reusable energy-absorbing metamaterial whose dissipation rises with strain rate by a power law and reaches densities comparable to those of plastically deforming metals. Together, these results outline a path toward structural materials that adapt, reinforce, and protect autonomously, with implications ranging from orthopedic implants and marine structures to protective equipment and soft robotics. event.description: Paolo Decuzzi (Italian Institute of Technology and Stanford University) The therapeutic performance of drug delivery systems can be enhanced by tailoring the geometrical and mechanical properties of the carrier itself. event.description: The recent explosion of AI capacity, along with booming prophecies about its limitless potential, arrives at a moment of profound unease. Just over a century ago, in the aftermath of the First World War, W.B. Yeats gave poetic form to a similar anxiety. In The Second Coming, he described an old order unraveling; “the centre cannot hold,” and something new and uncertain is taking shape. He imagined this new revelation in the form of a sphinx, rising from the desert sand, its gaze “blank and pitiless as the sun,” and ended the poem wondering “what rough beast, its hour come round at last, / Slouches towards Bethlehem to be born?” Is AI, then, a new Copernican moment? Not because it moves us in the cosmos, but because it unsettles our sense of what makes us central, distinct, and human. What would it actually mean for AI to surpass us? We exercise judgment, form relationships, create culture, make meaning, and act from values and beliefs. As AI becomes more and more capable, which, if any, of these practices remain distinctly ours? Philosopher and responsible AI leader Ken Archer, who heads Responsible AI at Microsoft, and Jackson Kernion, who leads the human feedback program at Anthropic, join literary scholar and BKC Faculty Associate Moira Weigel to consider whether Yeats’ apocalyptic vision has become not just “rough,” but rogue — and whether it will leave, or already has left, humanity behind. This conversation launches All Too Human: How AI Is Changing the Ways We Make Meaning, a year-long series examining how AI is reshaping our relationships, beliefs and values, art and creativity, and our most intimate emotional experiences.
event.title: What Rough Beast...? On AI's Potential to Surpass Humanity

event.description: RSVP HERE A Harvard-China Project Research Seminar with Christian Kaps, Assistant Professor of Business Administration, Harvard Business School Abstract: Managing electricity demand is critical for lowering the cost of electrified products, integrating intermittent renewables, and reducing grid expansion needs. With its often flexible demand, electric vehicle (EV) charging has long been considered a promising candidate, yet many managed charging programs have not scaled. We analyze why this is the case and identify several challenges to existing programs, focusing on two business models: smart electricity consumption (V1G) and demand response (DR). After grounding the analysis in a stylized model, we leverage a longitudinal dataset of over 20,000 EVs and 1.5 million charging events across the U.S. to empirically study managed charging. We find that V1G with time-of-use pricing saves EV owners up to $300 annually but increases the utility's wholesale generation cost, a misalignment that in 75% of markets cannot be costs-effectively eliminated by paying owners to adjust charge timing. For DR, the top 10% of customers provide 5.2 times the average vehicle's value, and only 9.4% of vehicles can be profitably enrolled. We identify which charging behaviors predict profitable DR customers and how this interacts with utilities' prices. We further analytically show when V1G and DR may be misaligned, and show empirically that V1G participation cannibalizes 16-46% of DR returns, highlighting challenges with stacking value streams. event.description: AI and digital platforms promise a friction-free future, yet the systems taking shape around us depend on hidden human labor, powerful corporate interests, and business models that demand more and more of those they purport to serve. In Cory Doctorow’s formulation, the defining metaphor may not be the centaur—a human enhanced by a machine—but the “reverse centaur”: a person driven by the force of an an automated system. Join author and activist Cory Doctorow and Dr. Elizabeth Mynatt, Dean of Northeastern University’s Khoury College of Computer Sciences, for a conversation about the structural, economic, and human stakes of this reversal. Drawing on his work on platform “enshittification” fostered by corporate monopoly, Doctorow asks us to focus not only on what technology does, but whom it is done to, who benefits, and who bears its costs. Mynatt brings a human-centered computing perspective, considering how technologies can instead be designed around human needs, agency, and care. Together, they will explore a central challenge for AI development and governance: what legal, economic, and design choices can keep technology accountable to the people whose lives it shapes? What would it take to ensure that humans remain its beneficiaries, not its infrastructure? Copies of Enshittification: Why Everything Suddenly Got Worse and What To Do About It and The Reverse Centaur's Guide to Life After AI: How to Think About Artificial Intelligence—Before It's Too Late will be available for purchase.

event.description: A delicate balance of noncovalent interactions drives hydrated molecular amphiphile self-assembly into lyotropic liquid crystals (LLCs) of varied morphologies, with applications including nanoporous membranes, mesoporous material templates, and therapeutic delivery vehicles. Spherical micelles are intuitively anticipated to form high-symmetry close-packed and body-centered cubic (BCC) LLCs, by analogy to packings of “hard” (immutable) spheres. However, we have discovered that ionic surfactant micelles also form a variety of low-symmetry, tetrahedrally close-packed Frank–Kasper (FK) phases, each exhibiting discrete micelle size distributions. The spontaneous emergence of FK sigma, A15, C14, and C15 LLC phases arises from a frustrated noncovalent force balance that minimizes variations in amphiphile solvation, while maximizing electrostatic cohesion in the ionic micelle ensemble. We further describe how amphiphile structure and path-dependent processing of their aqueous dispersions drive LLC sphere packing symmetry selection, culminating in the discovery of aperiodically ordered lyotropic dodecagonal quasicrystals (DDQCs) in multiple amphiphile systems. Thus, these findings establish the ubiquity of complex (a)periodically ordered states in both hard and soft materials and suggest methods for producing them at larger length scales. event.description: Join us for our online seminar series event hosted by MIT Media Lab's Advancing Humans with AI (AHA) research program. This event features Ziv Epstein, Postdoctoral Associate at the MIT Schwarzman College of Computing. This session is a bonus addition to the AHA Seminar series, held in person on Friday, September 18, from 10:00 to 11:00 AM ET at the MIT Media Lab, 6F Lecture Hall 633 (E14-633), and streamed live online. It is co-hosted by Prof. Karrie Karahalios and AHA. Talks are all recorded and made available afterwards on YouTube, linked on each event webpage. Abstract Algorithmic amplifiers like social media and AI chatbots play an increasingly important role in how our society operates. But despite being built with noble intentions, these algorithmic systems have demonstrated a fundamental misalignment with their users' values: resulting in the amplification of low-quality information designed to reward, hack and sensationalize. In this talk, I'll discuss new ways to measure and steer algorithmic systems to align them with users' values. In a first series of lab and field experiments in the context of sharing misinformation on social media, I show that this can be mitigated by steering behavior via reminding people of their own values. In a second project, I introduce a novel personalization architecture for measuring the expression of basic human values. I will then apply it to a large-scale audit of X's ranking algorithm to reveal how subtle value tensions in users' engagement behavior produces a fundamental misalignment between algorithmic amplification and user's self-stated values. To close, I will discuss ongoing work on aligning AI systems for collective goals of diversity and autotelicity, focusing on the domain of human creativity and creative production.
